title: Yoruba Religion and the Orisha
objective: After this level you can explain how Yoruba tradition links a supreme God, the orisha and the ancestors, and what Ifa divination is.
summary: In Yoruba religion the Creator Olorun oversees hundreds of orisha, some of them deified ancestors, while Egungun festivals bring ancestors back. Ifa priests read signs linked to 256 odu.

cards.headline: 256 parts, with hundreds of verses each, chanted by Yoruba priests.
cards.body: That's the store of wisdom behind Ifa divination. First, meet the Creator, the orisha and the ancestors it belongs with.

cards.headline: One Creator, many orisha
cards.body: The Yoruba live mainly in southwestern Nigeria, with smaller groups in Benin and northern Togo. Many are now Christians or Muslims, but aspects of the traditional religion survive. In it, the Almighty Creator, Olorun, oversees the orisha, some 400 lesser gods and spirits. Devotion to the orisha is active and widespread, but Olorun has neither priests nor cult groups.

cards.headline: Three kinds of orisha
cards.body: Orisha fall into three overlapping kinds: primordial divinities, deified ancestors such as kings and city founders, and personified forces of nature. Shango is two at once: an early king of Oyo and a force of fire and lightning. Devotees turn to particular orisha for particular occupations, skills and problems.

cards.headline: The ancestors return
cards.body: Egungun masquerades, often performed at yearly festivals, honor the ancestors and seek blessings for the community. The costume, with gloves, foot covers and a mesh face screen, covers the performer and turns the wearer into a returned ancestor. At Qingming, families visit their ancestors. At Egungun, the ancestors visit.

cards.headline: Ifa: reading the signs
cards.body: The Yoruba regard Ifa, also called Orunmila, as the deity of wisdom. Ifa divination relies not on anyone's oracular powers but on signs read by a priest, the babalawo, with sacred palm nuts and a divination chain. Ifa's 256 odu each hold many verses, about 800, which the priests chant. Ifa is consulted when an important decision has to be made.

cards.headline: Yoruba Religion and the Orisha: the takeaways
learned: Olorun oversees the orisha, some 400 gods and spirits
Egungun festivals bring the ancestors back
Ifa priests read signs linked to 256 odu

questions.prompt: Who reads the signs in Ifa divination?

options.label: The person asking the question, alone

questions.explanation: The babalawo reads signs with sacred palm nuts and a divination chain.

questions.prompt: How do Egungun masquerades bring the ancestors to the community?

options.label: By reading the ancestors' names aloud from wooden tablets on an altar
options.rationale: That's closer to a Chinese home altar.

options.label: A fully covered performer becomes a returned ancestor at a festival

questions.explanation: The costume covers the wearer completely, turning the performer into a returned ancestor who brings blessings.

questions.prompt: Level 2's Edward Tylor defined religion as belief in spiritual beings. How does Yoruba tradition fit that definition?

options.label: It fits poorly because it has no gods
options.rationale: It has a Creator and some 400 orisha.

options.label: It fits only because Yoruba people count in Pew surveys
options.rationale: Tylor's test is belief, not counting.

options.label: It doesn't fit, because orisha are only historical kings
options.rationale: Orisha include divinities and forces of nature.

options.label: It centers on a Creator and orisha, gods and spirits

questions.explanation: Olorun and the orisha, some 400 gods and spirits, are exactly the kind of content Tylor's substantive definition names.
